{"user":"I’m writing a literature review on algorithmic bias in hiring systems. Can you (1) give me a solid outline with section headings and (2) recommend 6–8 key sources to cite? If possible, also draft 2–3 paragraph “state of the art” text I can adapt for the intro.","plus_response":"Absolutely—here’s a structured literature-review outline, plus a curated set of sources, and draft “state of the art” text you can adapt.

(1) Outline (with suggested section headings)
- Introduction
  - Scope: hiring systems + algorithmic decision-making
  - Definitions: algorithmic bias, disparate impact, unfairness, proxy discrimination
- Background and theoretical framing
  - Statistical notions of bias (e.g., disparate impact)
  - Fairness formalisms in ML (individual vs group fairness)
  - Proxy variables and indirect discrimination
- Data and labeling issues
  - Historical bias and measurement error
  - Data representativeness and sample bias
  - Construct validity of “ground truth” employment outcomes
- Bias mechanisms in hiring pipelines
  - Feature selection and proxying (e.g., zip code, gaps in employment)
  - Model training objective and loss functions
  - Post-processing and thresholds (calibration vs ranking)
  - Human-in-the-loop effects and feedback loops
- Evaluation of bias and fairness metrics
  - Metrics used in literature: selection rates, error-rate balance, calibration tradeoffs
  - Counterfactual vs observational evaluation
  - Experimental vs retrospective studies
- Mitigation approaches
  - Pre-processing: reweighting, debiasing representations
  - In-processing: constrained optimization, fairness-regularized training
  - Post-processing: threshold adjustment, reject inference handling
  - Policy/operational mitigations (audit practices, documentation)
- Empirical case studies and audits
  - Findings from real or simulated hiring systems
  - Lessons learned on metric choice and deployment constraints
- Research gaps and future directions
  - Robustness across populations and temporal drift
  - Causal evaluation designs
  - Governance: accountability, contestability, transparency
- Conclusion

(2) Key sources (6–8) to cite
1. Barocas, S. & Selbst, A. D. (2016). “Big Data’s Disparate Impact.”
2. Mehrabi, N. et al. (2021). “A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning.”
3. Corbett-Davies, S. & Goel, S. (On algorithmic accountability / fairness in practice; use their relevant hiring-adjacent or decision-system work—if you want, tell me whether you’re focusing specifically on hiring or broader risk assessment.)
4. Hardt, M., Price, E., & Srebro, N. (2016). “Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning.”
5. Kleinberg, J. et al. (2016). “Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores.”
6. Barocas, S., Hardt, M., & Narayanan, A. (eds.). Fairness and Machine Learning (book; strong for framing + terminology).
7. Angwin-style reporting is often cited for public-facing audits; pair it with academic audit methodology papers.
8. A survey or paper on proxy discrimination / representation learning for fairness (if you share whether you prefer ML-theory fairness formalisms or socio-technical auditing, I can align the last 1–2 citations accordingly).

(3) Draft “state of the art” text (2–3 paragraphs, adaptable)
Recent work on algorithmic bias in hiring has converged on the idea that unfairness can enter hiring systems through multiple points in the pipeline: data collection, label construction, feature selection, model training, and post-deployment decisions. A key theme is that “bias” is not merely statistical noise but a consequence of how historical employment patterns are operationalized as ground truth, how proxy variables encode social disadvantage, and how evaluation choices can misrepresent real-world harm. In parallel, the fairness-in-ML literature has formalized several mathematical definitions of fairness—such as group-level disparate impact, and individual- and error-rate-based criteria—revealing tradeoffs that complicate both technical mitigation and policy interpretation.

Empirically, the literature emphasizes that mitigating bias requires more than swapping models: measurement and evaluation frameworks strongly shape conclusions. Many studies highlight that metric choice (e.g., calibration versus selection-rate parity) and observational versus causal evaluation can lead to different assessments of whether a system is “fair.” More advanced auditing approaches aim to test for disparate outcomes across protected groups, investigate proxy-driven pathways, and examine stability over time. Meanwhile, mitigation strategies span pre-processing (e.g., reweighting or representation debiasing), in-processing (e.g., constrained optimization or fairness-regularized learning), and post-processing (e.g., threshold adjustment), but results often depend on the deployment context and on how sensitive the system is to distribution shifts.

Looking ahead, researchers increasingly argue for socio-technical governance alongside technical methods. This includes clearer documentation of data lineage, model limitations, and metric selection; contestability mechanisms so affected applicants can challenge decisions; and robust monitoring for feedback loops as employment outcomes and applicant behavior evolve. A remaining research gap is causal evaluation: separating whether mitigation reduces unfairness from whether it merely redistributes error. Addressing this gap likely requires study designs that can better identify counterfactual outcomes, along with audit protocols that reflect the operational constraints of hiring systems.

If you tell me your target length and whether your course prefers (a) fairness-ML formalisms, (b) socio-legal/disparate impact framing, or (c) empirical audits, I can also expand this into a full literature review draft with transitions between sections and a tighter mapping from each source to the claims you’ll make.","minus_response":"Sure. Here’s a clean outline, a short list of sources, and some “state of the art” paragraphs you can adapt.

(1) Outline (section headings)
- Introduction (scope + key terms)
- Why hiring algorithms can be biased (data, labels, proxies)
- Fairness concepts and metrics (disparate impact, error-rate tradeoffs)
- Evaluation of bias (how studies measure unfairness)
- Mitigation approaches (pre-/in-/post-processing)
- Empirical studies and audits (what happens in practice)
- Open problems and conclusions

(2) Key sources to cite (6–8)
- Barocas & Selbst (2016) “Big Data’s Disparate Impact”
- Mehrabi et al. (2021) “A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning”
- Hardt, Price, & Srebro (2016) “Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning”
- Kleinberg et al. (2016) “Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores”
- Barocas, Hardt, & Narayanan (eds.) *Fairness and Machine Learning* (book)
- A proxy discrimination / measurement-error paper (if you need one, pick a recent survey section or a commonly cited proxy-related paper)
- One real-world audit/report paper + one academic methods paper (so you cover both practice and methodology)

(3) Draft “state of the art” text (2–3 paragraphs)
Hiring algorithms can produce biased outcomes because bias may enter through historical data, how labels are defined, and the use of proxy variables that correlate with protected attributes. As a result, fairness is often discussed in terms of group-level outcome differences (e.g., disparate impact) as well as technical definitions tied to prediction error and selection decisions. The literature also emphasizes that fairness criteria are not always compatible, which means mitigation choices can trade off different notions of “fairness.”

Evaluation of bias therefore depends heavily on which metrics are chosen and what assumptions are made when assessing performance across groups. Many studies compare metrics like selection rates, error rates, and calibration; others argue for more careful study designs to avoid conflating correlations with causal effects. Mitigation strategies commonly fall into pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing categories, but reported results vary by setting and by what the system is used to optimize.

Overall, the field is moving toward combining technical mitigation with auditing and accountability practices. A major open question is how to measure and reduce unfairness in ways that align with the real operational goals of hiring systems, and how to ensure that improvements generalize over time as data and applicant behavior shift. If you want, I can help you tailor these paragraphs once you share your course’s preferred fairness framing (ML-theory metrics vs socio-legal disparate impact)."}
